title: RLC Circuits
short: The same equation as a damped spring, in electrical form.

blocks.html: A series circuit with an inductor $L$, a resistor $R$ and a capacitor $C$ obeys the same equation as a damped spring. Everything from free vibrations and resonance carries over, with new names.

With charge $q(t)$ and current $i = q'$: $$Lq'' + Rq' + \frac{1}{C}q = E(t).$$ Natural frequency $\omega_0 = \frac{1}{\sqrt{LC}}$; underdamped when $R^{2} < \frac{4L}{C}$, critically damped when $R^{2} = \frac{4L}{C}$, overdamped when $R^{2} > \frac{4L}{C}$.

blocks.cap: The dictionary between the two systems.

blocks.html: Kirchhoff's voltage law: around the loop, the voltage drops add up to the source voltage. The drops are $L\frac{di}{dt}$ across the inductor, $Ri$ across the resistor and $\frac{q}{C}$ across the capacitor. With $i = q'$ this is $Lq'' + Rq' + \frac{q}{C} = E$. The inductor resists changes in current the way mass resists changes in velocity, and the capacitor pushes back in proportion to its charge the way a spring does.

blocks.html: Writing the damping test as $R^{2} < 4LC$. In the dictionary, $k$ corresponds to $\frac{1}{C}$, so $c^{2} < 4mk$ becomes $R^{2} < \frac{4L}{C}$. A units check helps: $\frac{L}{C}$ has units of ohms squared.

blocks.cap: The spring picture of the first example: “mass” $L = 1$, “damping” $R = 2$, “stiffness” $\frac{1}{C} = 5$. The height shows $q - 2$, the charge measured from its final value $CE = 2$. Raise the damping to see the circuit become overdamped.
